title: Putting safeguards in place
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: Safeguarding policy contents; review one year after first writing, then every three years or after law changes; procedures topics (trips, codes of conduct, online safety, photography, transport, ratios); clubs need a welfare or safeguarding officer; no formal safeguarding qualification is currently required. Opened with WebFetch. The old thecpsu.org.uk address redirects here.

title: Role description: club welfare officer (last updated 22 Oct 2024)
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: The club welfare officer is the first point of contact for concerns, keeps contact details for children's social care, police and the LADO, reports to regional or national leads, and is not expected to have a social worker's or police officer's knowledge. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Deal with a concern
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: Immediate danger: call 999; you do not need to decide whether abuse happened before reporting; NGB route (club welfare officer, lead safeguarding officer, LADO or police); non-NGB route (NSPCC Helpline 0808 800 5000, help@nspcc.org.uk, children's social care, police 101); Childline 0800 1111. No page date shown. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Guidelines on staffing and supervision ratios for children's activities (updated 5 Feb 2026)
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: Recommended minimum ratios by age (4-8 years 1:6, 9-12 1:8, 13-18 1:10), at least two adults, usually at least one first-aid trained, factors that raise supervision; guidance, not law, but part of the duty of care. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Online safety in sport (last updated 14 Feb 2025)
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: No private messages from staff to a young person; no one-to-one contact on encrypted platforms; public groups or via parents; agreed hours; risk-assess sport apps such as Spond and Teamo; two staff with access to social media accounts; live sessions with a parent present and two staff. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Photography and filming in sports and activities (last updated 28 Oct 2026)
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: Parent or carer consent under 16, ask the child too, consent can be withdrawn; no names or training times with images; organisation-owned devices only; no photography in changing rooms, toilets or first aid areas; AI manipulation risk. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Safer recruitment (last updated 8 Jan 2021)
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: Safer recruitment for paid and unpaid roles: self-declaration, at least two interviewers, two written references, identity checks, DBS (England and Wales), AccessNI, Disclosure Scotland, safeguarding training within six months, probation. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Parents and carers in sport (last updated 13 May 2025)
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: What to share with parents at the start of a season (ethos, rules, contact point, parents' code of conduct, how to raise concerns, coaching values); encourage positive involvement; boundaries on coach time. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Using AI responsibly in youth sport (last updated 19 Feb 2026)
publisher: NSPCC Child Protection in Sport Unit (CPSU)
supports: AI use must meet UK GDPR and ICO guidance (Children's Code for tools used by under-18s); DPIAs and an AI-use register; least intrusive option; humans make important decisions; risk of staff pasting sensitive data into public AI tools; coaches and welfare officers follow the AI policy and seek approval before adopting new AI tools. Opened with WebFetch.

title: DBS checks in sport: working with children (updated 17 Sep 2026)
publisher: Disclosure and Barring Service, GOV.UK
supports: Coaches who teach, train or instruct children on more than 3 days in any 30, or overnight between 2am and 6am, are eligible for an Enhanced check with a Children's Barred List check; applies to paid and unpaid roles; asking for one makes the club a regulated activity provider. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Circular 005/2022: Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022
publisher: Home Office and Ministry of Justice, GOV.UK
supports: Section 47 inserts s22A into the Sexual Offences Act 2003, extending position of trust offences to adults who regularly coach, teach, train, supervise or instruct an under-18 in a sport; commenced 28 June 2022; England and Wales. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Code of Practice for Sports Coaches
publisher: UK Coaching
supports: Four areas (personal standards, professional standards, relationships, rights); keep records of participants' progress; refer to other specialists when needed; act on safeguarding concerns; position of trust rules for 16 and 17 year olds. No version date on page. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Duty to Care
publisher: UK Coaching
supports: Six pillars: diversity, inclusion, mental health and well-being, physical well-being, safeguarding, safe to practice. No launch date on page. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Coach Learning Framework
publisher: UK Coaching
supports: Five principles for learning environments: holistic, flexible, person-centred, long-term, connected; balance of challenge and support. No date on page. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Understanding the Duty of Care and Negligence (dated 21 Aug 2026)
publisher: UK Coaching
supports: Coaches owe a legal duty of care judged against accepted practice (Bolam test), NGB guidelines and ratios; plan progressions and judge readiness by competence, not age band alone; stop and remove an injured participant; keep coaching plans showing progressions. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Coaching in the UK 2024: Coaches written report
publisher: UK Coaching with YouGov
supports: Online survey of 30,990 UK adults, 1 May to 7 June 2024: 6% coached in the last 12 months (about 3.2 million active coaches); 53% of active coaches paid in any capacity (22% paid only, 31% paid and voluntary); 26% coach older children (10-13) and 25% young people (14-17). PDF opened and converted to text.

title: Long-Term Development in Sport and Physical Activity 3.0 (2019)
publisher: Sport for Life Society
supports: Stages and approximate ages (Active Start, FUNdamentals, Learn to Train, Train to Train and later); 22 key factors including developmental age, sensitive periods, excellence takes time (8 to 12 years), appropriate specialisation (not before early teens except gymnastics, figure skating, diving), training-to-competition ratios; informal competition with no recorded results at FUNdamentals; Learn to Train estimated 70% training and 30% competition. PDF opened and converted to text.

title: UK Concussion Guidelines for Non-Elite (Grassroots) Sport (November 2024 update)
publisher: Sport and Recreation Alliance with the UK Government
supports: First published April 2023, updated November 2024. If in doubt, sit them out; recognise, remove, return; no return within 24 hours; NHS 111 within 24 hours; 999 for red flags; 24-48 hours relative rest; six-stage graduated return to activity and sport; full training not before day 15; competition not before day 21 and only after 14 days symptom-free at rest; GP if symptoms last over 28 days; children may take longer; for primary school age upwards; not medical advice. Page opened with WebFetch; the linked PDF was opened and converted to text.

title: Concussion Signs and Symptoms (dated 15 Sep 2025)
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), HEADS UP
supports: Signs coaches and parents see, symptoms athletes report, danger signs that need 911 or the emergency department; signs may not show up right away. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Responding to a Sports-related Concussion (dated 15 Sep 2025)
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), HEADS UP
supports: Remove from play, emergency department for danger signs, keep out the same day and until a healthcare provider clears them; adults should not judge severity; return is a medical decision. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Returning to Sports and Activities (dated 15 Sep 2025)
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), HEADS UP
supports: Six-step return with a healthcare provider's approval and supervision; each step usually at least 24 hours; stop and contact the provider if symptoms return. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Preventing Concussion (dated 15 Sep 2025)
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), HEADS UP
supports: Limit contact practices in contact and collision sports; enforce the rules; praise athletes who report symptoms; build a safe sport culture. Opened with WebFetch.

title: HEADS UP to Youth Sports Coaches: Online Concussion Training (dated 15 Sep 2025)
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), HEADS UP
supports: Online concussion training for youth sports coaches: signs and symptoms, the coach's role in removing an athlete, steps after a possible concussion; hosted on CDC TRAIN. Opened with WebFetch.

title: 2025 Minor Athlete Abuse Prevention Policies (MAAPP), effective 1 January 2025
publisher: U.S. Center for SafeSport
supports: Required for the USOPC, NGBs and local affiliated organisations; minor athlete means under 18; one-on-one contact observable and interruptible; electronic communications open and transparent with a parent or another adult copied, including team messages; recommended 8 am to 8 pm; no private social media connections; one-on-one transport needs annual written parent consent or another adult or two minors aged 8 or over; Core training before regular contact or within 45 days, refresher every 12 months, Core again every four years. PDF opened and converted to text.

title: Report a Concern
publisher: U.S. Center for SafeSport
supports: Report suspected child abuse to local authorities first, then the Center; 911 in an emergency; phone 833-587-7233; exclusive authority over sexual misconduct in the Olympic and Paralympic Movement, none over non-Movement leagues or non-Olympic sports; mandatory reporters must follow state law. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Recognising and responding to abuse (last updated 6 Nov 2025)
publisher: NSPCC Learning
supports: When a child discloses: listen calmly and let them go at their own pace, never promise to keep it secret, write down their exact words, separate fact from opinion, follow the organisation's procedures as soon as possible, call 999 if a child is in immediate danger. The page notes some sections are under review after changes from September 2026. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Overuse Injuries, Overtraining, and Burnout in Young Athletes (Brenner and Watson, Pediatrics 153(2), 2024), Europe PMC record
publisher: American Academy of Pediatrics, via Europe PMC
supports: Abstract: overuse injuries come from repetitive stress without enough recovery; overtraining harms performance and health; burnout is a leading reason young people leave sport. The publisher page blocks fetching, so the abstract was read from the Europe PMC record. Opened with WebFetch.

title: The fun integration theory: toward sustaining children and adolescents sport participation (Visek et al., Journal of Physical Activity and Health, 2015)
publisher: PubMed Central
supports: Concept mapping with youth soccer players, coaches and parents: 81 fun-determinants in 11 dimensions; the highest-rated dimensions were being a good sport, trying hard and positive coaching. Full text opened with WebFetch.

title: Children's activity levels rising, inactivity remains too high (Active Lives Children and Young People 2024-25, published 4 Dec 2025)
publisher: Sport England
supports: 49.1% of children aged 5-16 in England active for 60+ minutes a day, the Chief Medical Officers' guideline; 28.4% less active (under 30 minutes); survey of over 100,000 children. Opened with WebFetch.

title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation)
publisher: EUR-Lex, Publications Office of the European Union
supports: Article 4(15) defines data concerning health; Article 9 makes it a special category with conditions such as explicit consent; Article 8 sets 16 as the age for a child's own consent to online services, with member states free to lower it to no less than 13; Recital 38 on children's data. Opened with WebFetch.
